title: "🔗 Cross-Course Connections"
subtitle: "Where IR 362, ECON 205, and ACCT 410x reinforce each other"
description: "Same week of finals — make the courses talk to each other"
---

::: {.thesis}
**Why this page exists.** You're studying three courses in the same week. They look unrelated. They are not. The same idea — *measurement, distortion, equilibrium* — runs through all three. Studying them together is faster than studying them apart, because each course gives you a different vocabulary for the same underlying concept. Use this page on your second pass, after the cram sheets.
:::

## IR 362 ↔ ECON 205

::: {.connection-card}
### Oil rents and the resource curse

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**IR 362** — Mitchell's *Carbon Democracy*; Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds' "oil + hereditary executive"; rentier-state logic:::
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — natural-resource curse; the Dutch Disease channel; resource exports → currency appreciation → manufacturing decline:::
:::

**Why both at once.** Hammad treats oil as a *political* infrastructure that produces authoritarian robustness. ECON 205 treats oil as an *export* that distorts the exchange-rate channel and sterilizes industrial diversification. They are the **same fact** from different sides: oil rents lower the political cost of repression *and* the economic incentive to industrialize. Once you see this, "Why didn't the Gulf states transition in 2011?" and "Why is Saudi GDP composition unusual?" are the same question.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Write three sentences. (1) Use Mitchell to explain why MENA oil makes regime change rare. (2) Use the resource-curse / exchange-rate channel from ECON Ch 19 to explain why MENA oil makes manufacturing rare. (3) Connect them: the *political* and *economic* effects of oil rents are the same mechanism in two vocabularies.
:::
:::

::: {.connection-card}
### Sanctions on Iran and the trade/finance channels

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**IR 362** — sanctions as a tool of US primacy; JCPOA 2015 as relief; "maximum pressure" 2018+; Iran's adaptation via the axis of resistance:::
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — Ch 18 (trade): tariffs, quotas, embargoes shrink trade volumes; Ch 19 (finance): capital-account controls, currency depreciation, parallel exchange rates:::
:::

**Why both at once.** Sanctions are a *political* instrument with a clean *economic* signature. ECON 205 gives you the supply/demand graph of an embargo (DWL triangles, the rent rectangle going to license-holders or smugglers); IR 362 gives you the strategic intent (forcing a regime to the bargaining table; degrading proxy financing). The 2015 JCPOA is the moment both vocabularies briefly aligned — sanctions relief was *measurable* in oil exports and *visible* in Iran's regional reach.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Draw a simple supply-demand graph for Iranian oil under sanctions. Label the DWL, the rent rectangle, and the deadweight loss to global consumers. Then write one sentence explaining why this *graph* is what Hammad means when he calls sanctions "a structural constraint on Iran's regional engine."
:::
:::

::: {.connection-card}
### Gulf currency pegs and fixed exchange rates

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**IR 362** — GCC dollar pegs as a security signal — alignment with US financial system; cost of breaking the peg = exit from US-led order:::
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — Ch 19: fixed exchange rates, the "trilemma" (you can have any two of: fixed FX, free capital, independent monetary policy); PPP and real exchange-rate divergence:::
:::

**Why both at once.** A currency peg is *both* a monetary regime and a foreign-policy posture. ECON tells you what the peg costs (loss of independent monetary policy; vulnerability to speculative attack); IR tells you why Gulf states pay that cost anyway (alignment-signaling, capital-market access, predictable trade with the dollar bloc). The Saudi-Iran rapprochement (3/2023) and any post-Accords realignment will *show up first* in pressure on the peg — that's where the two courses converge.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Suppose Saudi inflation runs 3pp above US inflation for five years. Using PPP, what should happen to the riyal nominally? What actually happens (peg)? Then explain in one sentence what political work the peg is doing that the macro identity can't see.
:::
:::

## IR 362 ↔ ACCT 410x

::: {.connection-card}
### Egypt's military economy as a financial-statement reading exercise

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**IR 362** — Sayigh (Carnegie 2019): the Egyptian military runs **~25% of government spending**; opaque, off-balance-sheet, immune from civilian audit:::
::: {.term}**ACCT 410x** — ratio analysis, statement of cash flows, the indirect method; the question of *what's actually in* a reported number:::
:::

**Why both at once.** ACCT 410x trains you to read a financial statement and ask "what's missing, what's reclassified, what's a non-cash item, what's allocated vs. avoidable?" Sayigh is doing exactly that for a *country*. When 25% of an "income statement" is one entity that doesn't get audited, every ratio (profit margin, ROA, debt-to-assets) is meaningless until you adjust for that entity. The IR 362 frame and the ACCT 410x toolkit are the same frame: *don't trust the headline number*.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Imagine Egypt's general government as a corporation. Write a one-paragraph "earnings quality" memo: (a) what segment dominates "revenue" or "spending," (b) what disclosure is missing, (c) which ratios you would refuse to compute without a footnote, (d) what the analyst's hedge would be. Then read it back as commentary on Sisi-era political economy.
:::
:::

::: {.connection-card}
### Crony capitalism as a margin-and-allocation problem

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**IR 362** — Diwan/Malik/Atiyas: crony capitalism reduces *aggregate* growth (not just redistributes); networked firms get tariff protection, contracts, credit:::
::: {.term}**ACCT 410x** — relevant costs; "ignore allocated fixed costs that don't change"; how reported margins overstate efficiency when subsidies are bundled in:::
:::

**Why both at once.** The Diwan/Malik/Atiyas claim is, in accounting language: connected firms have *artificially low* costs (subsidized inputs, allocated fixed costs they don't bear) and *artificially high* margins. Their reported profitability is not real economic profit — it's a transfer. The 410x lesson "ignore sunk costs and reallocated FC" is the *same skill* as Diwan's lesson "don't read state-firm profitability as productivity."

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** A connected firm reports a 30% gross margin. The unconnected competitor in the same sector reports 8%. Using ACCT 410x cost categories (variable, fixed-but-allocated, opportunity cost), list three line items where the gap is *not* productivity. Then write one sentence on what this implies for IR 362's "aggregate growth" claim.
:::
:::

## ECON 205 ↔ ACCT 410x

::: {.connection-card}
### GDP measurement and accounting income measurement

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — Ch 5–6: spending GDP $Y = C + I + G + NX$; nominal vs real; deflator; double-counting avoided by using *value-added*:::
::: {.term}**ACCT 410x** — accrual basis: revenue when *earned*, expense when *incurred*; matching principle; net income as a constructed number:::
:::

**Why both at once.** GDP is to a country what net income is to a firm: a *constructed* aggregate that requires choices about timing, scope, and measurement. Both face the same traps — what counts as "production" vs. "transfer," when do you recognize an event, how do you handle non-cash flows. The intuition that builds in 410x ("Unearned Revenue is a liability until it's earned") is the same intuition that builds in 205 ("government transfers are not GDP").

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Take three transactions and classify them in *both* frameworks. (1) US government pays $1B in Social Security: GDP impact? Accounting income impact for a recipient household? (2) Apple sells $1B in iPhones, half on credit due next quarter: GDP impact this quarter? Accrual revenue this quarter? Cash flow this quarter? (3) A factory destroyed by fire: GDP impact? Accounting impact (loss recognition)?
:::
:::

::: {.connection-card}
### Inflation and inventory accounting

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — Ch 11: inflation reduces purchasing power; Fisher (real vs nominal); creditors lose / debtors gain on unexpected inflation:::
::: {.term}**ACCT 410x** — FIFO vs LIFO under rising prices; LIFO → higher COGS → lower NI → lower tax; FIFO → ending inventory at *current* costs:::
:::

**Why both at once.** Inflation is a measurement problem. ECON 205 tells you that nominal numbers mislead in real terms; ACCT 410x tells you that inventory cost-flow assumptions *react* to that misleading. Under rising prices, LIFO is "more conservative" precisely because it pushes recent (high) costs into COGS, matching today's revenue with today's costs — that's the matching principle doing inflation-adjustment by hand. FIFO leaves inventory holding gains in net income; LIFO doesn't.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Assume 10% inflation and rising input prices. (a) Compute the difference between FIFO NI and LIFO NI for a firm with $100k beginning inventory rolling to $110k ending inventory. (b) Using Fisher, explain *which* of the two NI numbers is closer to "real" income. (c) Connect this to ECON 205's claim that inflation redistributes from creditors to debtors — which inventory method makes the firm look more like a creditor, and which like a debtor?
:::
:::

::: {.connection-card}
### Fed monetary policy and corporate financing decisions

::: {.terms}
::: {.term}**ECON 205** — Ch 16: Fed buys/sells bonds → r changes; bond price ↔ yield inverse; transmission to I, C, NX; Taylor Rule:::
::: {.term}**ACCT 410x** — bond pricing direction: market rate > coupon → discount; market rate < coupon → premium; the carrying value drifts toward face:::
:::

**Why both at once.** The bond pricing logic in ACCT 410x is the *same equation* the Fed is using on the macro side. When the Fed raises rates (ECON 205), every outstanding fixed-coupon corporate bond's market price falls (ACCT 410x). The discount/premium classification on the issuer's books is just the firm-level version of "where is the market rate today vs. when we issued this." If you can answer "what does the Fed's rate hike do to AD?" *and* "what does it do to bonds payable on a balance sheet?" with the same intuition, you have both courses' Ch-16-equivalent material in one mental model.

::: {.exercise}
**Bridge exercise.** Suppose the Fed hikes 100bp. (a) ECON 205: trace AD/AS to predict P, Y. (b) ACCT 410x: a 5-year, 4% coupon corporate bond was issued at par yesterday. What's the new market price direction, and how does the issuing firm's interest expense change going forward (it doesn't — explain why). (c) One sentence connecting them.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**The meta-lesson.** All three courses are about *measurement under distortion*. IR 362 measures regional power when actors lie about it; ECON 205 measures real activity when prices distort it; ACCT 410x measures firm performance when timing and allocation distort it. The student who walks into these three exams treating them as one *measurement* exam will out-perform the student who treats them as three separate sets of facts.
:::
